easy.heading: Warming Up With a Few Doubles
easy.body:
Hey there! I am so glad you dropped by. I just finished my morning coffee and today's Pips was a real treat to wake up to. I started the easy puzzle by looking for the biggest numbers first. I noticed a sum region at the bottom left, cells [2,0] and [2,1], that needed to add up to 10. Scanning my dominoes, the double fives [5,5] stood out immediately. It was the only way to hit that target, so I plopped it right in there.

After that, I looked at the top right where we had an equals sign between [0,3] and [1,3]. I also had a sum of 13 to find for the vertical line at [0,2], [1,2], and [2,2]. By placing the [6,0] domino across the top at [0,2] and [0,3], things started to click. That put a 6 in [0,2] and a 0 in [0,3]. Since [1,3] had to equal [0,3], it also became a 0. This left me needing a 7 from the remaining cells in that sum region, which I finished off using the [4,4] and [3,1] dominoes. It felt so satisfying to see the whole board just fall into place like that!

medium.heading: Navigating the Empty Spaces
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today was a bit of a jump in logic, but nothing we can't handle together. The most helpful clue for me was the empty constraint at [4,3]. In Pips, that usually means we are looking for a zero or a blank. I looked at my dominoes and saw the [6,0] piece. I decided to try placing it at [4,2] and [4,3]. This worked out perfectly because the sum of [4,1] and [4,2] had to be 7. If [4,2] was 6, then [4,1] only needed to be 1.

This led me to the [1,2] domino. I placed it at [4,0] and [4,1], which put a 2 in the [4,0] spot. This was a lucky break because the target for cell [4,0] was exactly 2! From there, I worked my way up the board. The equals constraints at the top were a little tricky, but by using the [0,3] and [2,2] dominoes to balance the values, the rest of the tiles like the [4,1] and [6,2] pieces found their homes. It really shows how one small zero can help unlock the entire grid.

hard.heading: Tackling the Zero Zone
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today really made me think, but I found a great starting point that made it much easier. Down at the bottom, there is a region of three cells at [5,3], [6,3], and [6,4] that has a sum target of 0. That is a huge hint! It means every single one of those squares has to be a 0. I took the [0,0] domino and placed it at [6,3] and [6,4], then looked for another domino with a zero to cover [5,3].

Once that bottom section was anchored, I moved over to the sum of 9 at [4,0] and [5,0]. I used the [4,5] domino there, putting the 4 in the top spot and the 5 in the bottom. This helped me figure out the sum of 2 at [2,0] and [3,0]. I spent a little time guessing where the [1,6] and [3,6] dominoes might go, but once I realized the equals constraint at [4,5], [5,5], and [6,5] required the same value in all three spots, I was able to narrow it down to the double 4s and other matching pieces. It was like a giant game of logic tag!

explanation.tips: Try to look for the most restrictive rules first, like very large sums or regions that must equal zero. These give you an anchor so you are not just guessing. Also, remember that each domino can only be used once, so crossing them off as you go is a total lifesaver for the harder levels.
explanation.learned: Today I learned just how powerful the zero values are in this game. In both the medium and hard puzzles, finding where the blank sides of the dominoes went was actually more helpful than figuring out the big numbers. It is a good reminder to look for what is missing, not just what is there.

faqs.question: What does the empty type mean in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: The empty constraint type means the cell should have a value of zero or a blank pip. It is often the best place to start because it limits which dominoes you can use.

faqs.question: How do you solve the sum regions in Pips?
faqs.answer: To solve a sum region, add up the values of all the cells within that colored area. They must equal the target number shown in the corner of the region.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally in Pips?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes must always be placed either horizontally or vertically to cover two adjacent squares on the grid.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for the hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: The best strategy is to find regions with very low or very high targets. These usually have only one or two possible domino combinations, which helps you build a foundation for the rest of the board.

faqs.question: Are the dominoes the same for everyone in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: Yes, every player gets the same set of dominoes and the same puzzle layout each day, so you can compare your solutions with friends!
